# Command block overview

In this document, we will show how the different command blocks in datenanpassr work. 
There are the following keywords that you can use to enter the command blocks in your Excel mapping file:
```{r}
command_block_classes %>% excelish()
```

*The column* `"command_block"` *shows the class, which determines how 
datenanpassr parses the command block* (with `parse_command_args()`) *and 
then applies it on the data* (with `apply_command()`).

# Command block examples

```{r illustrate_cmd_block_fun, child="../man/fragments/illustrate_command_block.Rmd"}
```


## `#VARL`

```{r varl}
dat <- tibble(q1 = 4:6)

cdb_args_raw <- tibble(X1 = "#VARL", X2 = "q1", X3 = "assigned variable label")

illustrate_cmd_block(dat, cdb_args_raw)
```


Actually, this command does not change the values, but it assigns the variable 
label specified in column **C** of the command to the variable specified in 
column **B**.



## `#VALL`

```{r vall}
dat <- tibble(q1 = c(1, 1, 2))

cdb_args_raw <- tibble::tribble(
  ~X1, ~X2,            ~X3,
  "#VALL", "q1", "yes/no question",
   NA,  "1",     "Yes",
   NA,  "2", "No"
  )

illustrate_cmd_block(dat, cdb_args_raw)
```

This command also does not change the values. Just like `#VARL`, it assigns the variable label
specified in the first row of column **C** (if empty, it keeps the variable
label, if already existing) to the variable specified in the first row in column
**B**. It also assigns the value labels in column **C** to 
the values in column **B** in the following rows of the command.


## `#IF`

### Example

```{r if1}
dat <- tibble(q1 = 1:3)

cdb_args_raw <- tibble::tribble(
  ~X1, ~X2,            ~X3,
  "#IF", "q1 >= 2", "q2 = 5",
  )

illustrate_cmd_block(dat, cdb_args_raw)
```
This command takes a condition (more precisely a logical vector of length of the 
variables in the data) in column **B** and an assignment in column **C** (of the form 
`<variable name> = <assigned values>`). 
When the condition is `TRUE`, the expression (`<assigned values>`) is assigned 
to `<variable name>`.
In this case, the value 5 is assigned to `q2` where `q1` is greater or equal to 2.
In this case `q2` didn't exist in the data before, and thus is initialized to
`NA` before.

### Example

If the variable existed before, the values where the condition evalueates to `FALSE`
are kept, as can be seen in the next example:

```{r if2}
dat <- tibble(q1 = 1:3, q2 = c(7, 8, 9))

cdb_args_raw <- tibble::tribble(
  ~X1, ~X2,            ~X3,
  "#IF", "q1 >= 2", "q2 = 5",
  )

illustrate_cmd_block(dat, cdb_args_raw)
```

Here the value of 7 in the first row is kept from the original data.

### Example

The `#IF` command preserves labels, if an already existing variable is modified:

```{r if3}
dat <- tibble(q1 = haven::labelled(c(1, 2, 3), c(a = 1, b = 2, c = 3), "abc"))

cdb_args_raw <- tibble::tribble(
  ~X1, ~X2,            ~X3,
  "#IF", "q1 >= 2", "q1 = 5",
  )

illustrate_cmd_block(dat, cdb_args_raw)
```
